paras: The McGhee's Switch election intimidation took place at the Precinct No. 9 polling place at McGhee's Switch, Montgomery County, Alabama, on the night of the state election of August 2, 1880, when a militia company and an armed posse came to the polls and the Black Republican inspector, A. Oliver, was forced out of the vote count. Republican accounts said the ballot box was refilled in the dark after a candle was knocked over, producing a return of 540 Democratic votes. Northern Republican papers made it a leading example of Alabama election fraud; the militia's commander denied any intimidation.

In Montgomery County the Democratic sheriff and circuit clerk chose the election inspectors, and according to ex-Governor William H. Smith they named colored men as Republican inspectors while passing over white Republicans proposed by the probate judge. Because the precinct's vote had gone Democratic two years earlier, Republicans kept their own tally, which the Republican State Committee put at 672 votes. The committee added that one Democratic inspector, B. E. McGheehe, was under federal indictment for stuffing that earlier box.

According to Oliver's affidavit, the polls closed at 5 o'clock without trouble, but the Democratic inspectors would not begin the count until 7 p.m. Meanwhile, a federal judicial officer wrote, the deputy sheriff sent to Montgomery for help, and the governor ordered a detachment of the Montgomery Grays under Jones to the precinct. The committee said the inspectors had reported being threatened by the colored men waiting outside, and that the Grays arrived with about thirty armed citizens.

By 9 p.m., Oliver swore, 116 Republican and 55 Democratic ballots had been counted when the two Democratic inspectors stepped into an adjoining barroom. On their return Dr. McGee said the count "must be changed" and knocked over the candle; when a light was found, the box was fuller than before and tickets littered the floor. Oliver called it "an unfair deal," the inspectors cursed him, and McGee advanced on him "in a threatening manner," so that Oliver fled. He was refused re-entry, and the remaining inspectors finished the count. The Chicago Tribune's abstract of the committee address added that the militia drove away the Republicans waiting outside.

Smith sent Oliver's affidavit to Marshall Jewell, the national committee chairman, and proposed a bipartisan investigation. In September Paul Strobach of the Republican National Committee charged that the militia had been brought to terrorize the inspector. Capt. Thomas G. Jones, the company's commander, answered that it had gone to prevent "apprehended rioting," that none of his men but himself went within a quarter mile of the polls, and that he saw no intimidation. No report of arrests or prosecutions over the count appears in the coverage.

The first reports came from a Montgomery dispatch dated August 3, which the National Republican in Washington headed "Shameful Frauds in Alabama" and the Delaware Daily Republican "The Farce in Alabama"; the Phoenix Herald ran the same text. The dispatch said the Democrats meant to win "even to have democratic bayonets at the polls."

The New-York Tribune printed Smith's letter and Oliver's affidavit on August 14, and the Kenosha Telegraph copied the letter in September. The State Committee's address, which opened its list of frauds with this precinct, ran in late August in the Portland Daily Press, the New-York Tribune and the Burlington Free Press. Its text mocked the inspectors' fears, asking how 132 colored men could "terrorize 540 Democrats, white and black," while the Chicago Tribune called the Alabama frauds "infamous."
By late September the Omaha Bee cited "the outrage at McGhees' switch" as a byword, while the Democratic New York Sun printed Strobach's charge only beside Jones's denial.

Accounts differ on the armed force: the committee put the Grays and about thirty citizens there before the count, while Oliver described a deputy sheriff with about twenty-five citizens and twenty-three militiamen appearing after sundown. The Republican return was 132 in the committee's address but 13 in the Montgomery Advertiser figure Smith quoted. The inspectors' claim that Black voters had threatened them is known only through the committee; Oliver swore there had been no threats, though the judicial officer's letter called the Black men there "armed and determined."

reader.title: McGhee's Switch election intimidation
bases: A militia company and an armed citizens' posse were brought to a polling place during the count and the Black Republican inspector was cursed, threatened and kept out of the room; no one was reported hurt (A5, A9, A4).

Several separate Republican sources (a Montgomery dispatch, a federal judicial officer's letter, Oliver's affidavit, the State Committee address) agree that the militia and posse came and the inspector was forced out (A3, A4, A5, A9), and the militia commander confirms his company went there, but he denies any intimidation (A14).

accounts.label: Montgomery dispatch (Republican)
accounts.gist: About 600 Republican and 50 Democratic votes were polled; the candle was put out, the box refilled, the colored inspector driven out with curses, and a military company and armed posse under a deputy sheriff came though no trouble had occurred.

accounts.label: Federal judicial officer's letter
accounts.gist: The deputy sheriff wired the city for help, the governor sent Jones and the Grays, and the counting-out began on their arrival; Oliver was put out of the room for charging fraud.

accounts.label: Oliver's affidavit
accounts.gist: After 116 Republican and 55 Democratic votes were counted, Dr. McGee knocked over the candle, the box was refilled, Oliver was cursed and threatened and fled, and he was refused re-entry; the posse and militia appeared after sundown although there had been no trouble.

accounts.label: Republican State Committee address
accounts.gist: The inspectors delayed the count until the Grays and about 30 armed citizens arrived, claiming danger from the colored men waiting outside; the inspector was driven out and the return gave 132 to 540.

accounts.label: Militia commander's reply
accounts.gist: Capt. Thomas G. Jones said his company went under orders to prevent apprehended rioting, stayed a quarter mile from the polls except for himself, and intimidated no one.

framing.detail: Republican papers ran it under headlines such as 'Shameful Frauds in Alabama. How the Bourbons Carried the State—Outrageous Bulldozing and Stuffing' and 'The Farce in Alabama'.
The Chicago Tribune called the Alabama frauds 'infamous' and 'high-handed outrages', leading its abstract with McGehee's Switch.
The Democratic New York Sun printed Strobach's charge only with Jones's denial in a column of Hancock campaign news.
The Omaha Bee used 'the outrage at McGhees' switch' as a byword against the Democratic Omaha Herald.
